rich_summary: This section recounts the consequences of Bhishma’s terrible vow and the early succession struggles of the Kuru dynasty. To secure his father Santanu’s marriage to Satyavati, Devavrata renounces both the throne and all offspring, taking a lifelong vow of celibacy—an act so extreme that the gods name him Bhishma (“the Terrible”) and Santanu grants him the boon of choosing the time of his death. After Santanu’s death, Bhishma installs Satyavati’s son Chitrangada as king, but he is slain after a three‑year battle with a powerful Gandharva of the same name. The younger brother Vichitravirya becomes king under Bhishma’s guardianship. Seeking wives for him, Bhishma storms the swayamvara of the Kashi princesses and carries them away by force, defeating the assembled kings in a legendary display of martial prowess.

highlight_spans.why: The fisherman explains the political problem of rival heirs, setting up the demand that leads to Bhishma’s extraordinary vow.
Bhishma publicly renounces heirs and takes the vow of lifelong celibacy, the defining moment that shapes the future of the Kuru dynasty.
Santanu rewards Bhishma with the boon of choosing the moment of his own death—one of the most famous blessings in the epic.
The three‑year battle between Chitrangada and the Gandharva highlights the fragility of the Kuru line and the dangers of pride.
Bhishma’s speech on the forms of marriage precedes his dramatic abduction of the Kashi princesses, illustrating Kshatriya warrior customs.

top_scenes.scene_text: Devavrata stands before assembled kings and the fisherman, raising his hand as he vows lifelong celibacy while gods shower flowers and proclaim him Bhishma.
On the plains of Kurukshetra, Chitrangada battles the radiant Gandharva of the same name amid storms of weapons along the Saraswati river.
Bhishma drives away from the Kashi swayamvara with the three princesses on his chariot while dozens of furious kings pursue him in a blazing storm of arrows.
